content: The Stop TB Partnership was established in the year 2000 with the primary objective of eradicating tuberculosis (TB) as a public health issue and ultimately achieving a world free of TB. This partnership consists of a network of international organizations, countries, donors from both public and private sectors, governmental and non-governmental organizations, and individuals who have expressed a commitment to collaborate in achieving this goal. The origins of the Stop TB Initiative trace back to the First ad hoc Committee on the Tuberculosis Epidemic, which convened in London in March 1998. In March 2000, the initiative produced the Amsterdam Declaration to Stop TB, a pivotal moment in restructuring global efforts to combat TB. This declaration called for action from ministerial delegations of 20 countries with the highest TB burden. Later that year, the World Health Assembly endorsed the establishment of a Global Partnership to Stop TB and set two targets for 2005: diagnosing 70% of all individuals with infectious TB and curing 85% of those diagnosed. In October 2001, the Global Plan to Stop TB was launched, serving as the overarching framework for the partnership's collective actions. The Second Stop TB Partners' Forum, held in New Delhi in March 2004, resulted in the New Delhi Pledge, which reaffirmed ministerial commitments to meet the 2005 targets and to develop a second global plan to guide efforts toward achieving the Millennium Development Goals for TB by 2015. The Stop TB Partnership has evolved from its modest beginnings into a comprehensive global initiative. It brings together organizations and individuals dedicated to implementing both shortand long-term measures to control and eventually eliminate TB as a global public health problem. Partners have organized into Working Groups to accelerate progress in seven specific areas: DOTS Expansion, TB/HIV, MDR-TB, New TB Drugs, New TB Vaccines, New TB Diagnostics, and Advocacy, Communications, and Social Mobilization. These mechanisms have enabled the partnership to expand its reach, advance work plans, and support countries in accelerating their efforts against TB, as outlined in the Amsterdam Declaration. The Stop TB Partnership is a global movement aimed at expediting social and political action to halt the unnecessary spread of TB worldwide. The partnership has set specific targets: by 2005, 70% of people with infectious TB should be diagnosed, and 85% of them cured; by 2015, the global burden of TB (in terms of deaths and prevalence) should be reduced by 50% relative to 1990 levels; and by 2050, the global incidence of TB should be less than 1 case per million population, effectively eliminating TB as a global public health problem. The mission of the Stop TB Partnership is to ensure that every TB patient has access to effective diagnosis, treatment, and cure; to stop the transmission of TB; to reduce the inequitable social and economic burden of TB; and to develop and implement new preventive, diagnostic, and therapeutic tools and strategies to combat TB. To achieve this mission and realize its vision, the partnership has outlined several goals: promoting the wider and more effective use of existing strategies to interrupt TB transmission by increasing access to accurate diagnosis and effective treatments, accelerating DOTS implementation to meet global TB control targets, and improving the availability, affordability, and quality of anti-TB drugs. Additionally, the partnership aims to address emerging challenges such as MDR-TB and HIV-related TB by adapting DOTS to prevent and manage these threats. It also seeks to accelerate the elimination of TB by promoting research and development for new TB drugs, diagnostics, and vaccines, and by ensuring the adoption of new and improved tools through appropriate use, access, and affordability. The World Health Organization (WHO) plays a dual role in the Stop TB Partnership. As a leading agency within the partnership, WHO provides guidance on global policy and maintains permanent representation on the Stop TB Coordinating Board. Additionally, WHO serves as the housing institution for the Stop TB Partnership Secretariat, which benefits from WHO's administrative mechanisms. The secretariat adheres to WHO's rules and regulations for administrative, financial, and human resource management, with adaptations as necessary to meet the specific needs of the Stop TB Partnership.
